messages.content: For each integer \(s\ge 3\), let \(D_s\) be the least positive integer \(d\) with the following property: for every collection of \(2^s-2\) Borel probability measures on \(\mathbb R^d\), each absolutely continuous with respect to \(d\)-dimensional Lebesgue measure, there exist two affine hyperplanes whose complement has exactly four connected components, each having measure \(1/4\) for every measure in the collection. The same pair of hyperplanes must work for all the measures, and no perpendicularity condition is imposed. What is the exact value of \(D_s\) as a function of \(s\)?

content.text:
This is an open case of the **Grünbaum–Hadwiger–Ramos mass-partition problem**. In its standard notation,
\[
D_s=\Delta(2^s-2,2).
\]
No exact value is currently known for this family; already \(s=3\) asks for the unresolved value \(\Delta(6,2)\).

The established bounds are
\[
\boxed{\,3\cdot2^{s-1}-3\ \le D_s\le\ 3\cdot2^{s-1}-2\,}.
\]

For the lower bound, the standard moment-curve construction gives
\[
\Delta(j,2)\ge \left\lceil\frac{3j}{2}\right\rceil.
\]
Indeed, place the \(j\) measures on disjoint intervals of the moment curve. Four equal parts require at least three hyperplane crossings on each interval, whereas two hyperplanes have at most \(2d\) crossings altogether. Thickening the measures and taking a limit gives the same bound for absolutely continuous measures.

For the upper bound, the known general estimate
\[
\Delta(j,2)\le j+2^{\lfloor\log_2j\rfloor}
\]
gives the stated result when \(j=2^s-2\).

Ramos’s conjecture predicts the lower value,
\[
D_s\stackrel{?}{=}3\cdot2^{s-1}-3,
\]
but it is not established. In particular, the known bounds for \(D_3\) are \(9\le D_3\le10\).

from math import comb, gcd
j,d=6,9
# X=S^d x S^d; W=(R_A + R_B + R_C)^j.
# a and b flip the orientation of the first/second hyperplane;
# t exchanges the two hyperplanes.
orientation_X={'a':(-1)**(d+1),'b':(-1)**(d+1),'t':(-1)**(d*d)}
orientation_W={'a':((-1)*1*(-1))**j,'b':(1*(-1)*(-1))**j,'t':(-1)**j}
twist={g:orientation_X[g]*orientation_W[g] for g in orientation_X}
relations=[1-v for v in twist.values()]
modulus=gcd(*relations)
print('domain orientation character:',orientation_X)
print('target orientation character:',orientation_W)
print('top-degree local-coefficient twist:',twist)
print('coinvariant relations:',relations)
print('coinvariant group: Z/',modulus,'Z',sep='')
c=comb(j,j//2)//2
print('count =',c,'; mod 4 =',c%4,'; in obstruction coinvariants =',c%modulus)

### Why the modulo-four count does not prove existence

For six measures in dimension nine, parameterize oriented affine hyperplanes by \(S^9\). The configuration space is \(S^9\times S^9\), with the signed-permutation group generated by:
- \(a,b\), reversing the respective hyperplane orientations;
- \(\tau\), exchanging the hyperplanes.

The test representation is
\[
W=(\mathbb R_A\oplus\mathbb R_B\oplus\mathbb R_C)^{\oplus6},
\]
where \(A,B\) record the two bisection conditions and \(C\) records the product-sign condition.

The relevant orientation characters are
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
 &a&b&\tau\\ \hline
S^9\times S^9&+1&+1&-1\\
W&+1&+1&+1.
\end{array}
\]
Indeed, exchanging the two nine-dimensional factors reverses orientation, whereas exchanging the \(A,B\) coordinates in each of six representation blocks preserves orientation.

Consequently, in the top-degree obstruction calculation on the free part, exchange identifies an integer coefficient \(n\) with \(-n\). The resulting coefficient coinvariants are
\[
\mathbb Z/\langle n-(-n)\rangle\cong\mathbb Z/2,
\]
**not** \(\mathbb Z/4\).

Thus the count
\[
\frac12\binom63=10
\]
has zero image in the applicable obstruction group. Its residue \(2\pmod4\) supplies no additional obstruction: retaining an integer count modulo four is unjustified when the topological identifications retain only parity.

This vanishing does not prove that equipartitions fail—or that they exist. It only shows that this obstruction cannot close the gap.

The lower bound follows from the moment-curve construction, and the upper bound follows from the established estimate
\[
\Delta(j,2)\le j+2^{\lfloor\log_2j\rfloor}.
\]
Neither establishes the lower endpoint as the exact answer.
